Propriety
prō-prī´ĕ-ty
n. (fitness; accuracy; conformity to what is proper to a thing, an office or an occasion)
Latin proprietas, ownness, from proprius, one's own. Propriety is not politeness; it is the quality of a thing being proper to its subject — the right word, the right conduct, for this and not another.

Biblical Definition

Propriety is fitness to the case. Proverbs prizes it in speech: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11), and again, “a word spoken in due season, how good is it!” (Pro 15:23). Paul makes it a rule of conduct: “that women adorn themselves in modest apparel… which becometh women professing godliness” (1Ti 2:9–10), and of doctrine: “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1). Of the assembly he says only, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). And Proverbs notes what is not fitting: “Delight is not seemly for a fool; much less for a servant to have rule over princes” (Pro 19:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines propriety as fitness; suitableness; appropriateness; consonance with established principles, rules or customs; and accuracy, justness, as of words or language.

expand to see more

PROPRIETY, n. Property; peculiar or exclusive right of possession. [Obs.]

2. Fitness; suitableness; appropriateness; consonance with established principles, rules or customs; justness; accuracy.

Propriety of thought is that which is truly conformable to the subject.

Propriety of words is the peculiar and exclusive use of them to express a certain idea.

Key Scripture

Pro 25:11 — "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver."

Pro 15:23 — "A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!"

1Ti 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

Tit 2:1 — "But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:"

1Co 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Modern Corruption

Propriety is reduced to social convention, and Webster's own definition makes it a matter of truth: what is conformable to the subject.

expand to see more

Webster's line is the best short account of the word in English and it is not about manners at all: propriety of thought is that which is truly conformable to the subject. A proper word is one that fits the thing it names; a proper action is one that fits the case it answers. That makes propriety a species of honesty rather than of etiquette, and explains why Scripture treats it seriously. To speak of a grief in the language of a trifle, or of a trifle in the language of a grief, is a small lie about the world.

Proverbs 25:11 gives the picture and the emphasis falls on the adverb: a word fitly spoken. Not a true word merely, and not a kind word merely — the right word, at the right moment, in the right weight. Proverbs 15:23 adds the timing: a word spoken in due season, how good is it. Anyone who has been comforted well, or corrected well, knows that the content was often unremarkable and the fitness was everything; and anyone who has said the true thing at the wrong hour knows the cost.

The corruption to guard against is the use of propriety as a shield. Congregations have used it to silence honest grief, to forbid uncomfortable questions, and to enforce cultural preferences that have nothing to do with the gospel — and a great deal of what passes for decorum in church is simply the taste of whoever has been there longest. The test is Titus 2:1: speak the things which become sound doctrine. The standard is the doctrine, and a propriety that cannot be traced back to it is a custom, which may be kept or dropped as charity requires.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ophan (H655), fitly, in due manner; eth (H6256), season, time; Greek prepo (G4241), to be becoming; euschemonos (G2156), decently, becomingly.

expand to see more

Hebrew al-ophnav (H655) — fitly, upon its wheels, in due manner; Proverbs 25:11 only.

Greek prepo (G4241) — to be fitting, becoming; 1 Timothy 2:10, Titus 2:1, Ephesians 5:3, Hebrews 7:26.

Greek euschemonos (G2156) — decently, becomingly; 1 Corinthians 14:40, Romans 13:13, 1 Thessalonians 4:12.

Usage

"“A word fitly spoken” — and the adverb carries it."

"“Which become sound doctrine” — the standard, not the custom."

"“A word spoken in due season, how good is it!”"
